AlphaGo Zero is the one reference whose kind is left to inference. Since the article's argument depends on its network-versus-network selection step, the reader should be told plainly that it is a game-playing system. The two people in the Bitter Lesson section are lesser gaps.

# Review

## Placement and lifecycle

The article belongs in `kb/articles/`. It is an outward-facing explanation of a paradigm claim and an empirical bet. It links into the theory notes that carry the transferable claims, so it does not duplicate them. It is a `draft` at the collection root. It opens with an authored blockquote banner that says the claims and structure may change and names GitHub Discussions as the place to send comments. The banner promises no stability. The title is a reader-facing headline, not a claim title. The description works as an agent retrieval filter, and the opening paragraphs act as the reader's abstract.

## Linking and reader-only body

The body has no footer link tables, visible relation labels or graph-traversal glosses. In-prose links go only to authorized destinations: `kb/theory/` for definitions and arguments, `kb/sources/` for externally attributed claims (AlphaZero, PRODIGY, EURISKO, Greco et al., the harness-evolution study), and `kb/articles/` for companion articles. External links cover primary attribution: the AlphaGo Zero paper, Sutton's essay and the interview. Nothing points into `kb/work/` or into non-retained reports. The closing "Where to go next" section gives the onward path the quality goal asks for.

## Explanatory tests

A technical reader can state the two main claims, how they are supported and their material limits. The two claims are that selection needs a comparison, not a single score, and the bet that a fixed-weight LLM can build the preference model and make the robust comparison. The article gives no completed end-to-end run, five named hazards and an explicit failure condition. The routing-line example comes before the abstraction. "That sequence establishes three things" turns the example into general claims, and the robust-comparison and evidence sections return to the example. The gradient-training table, the precedent sequence and the Bitter Lesson section each advance the argument.

## Unmet conventions

Most of the gaps fall under the contract's rule against repeating qualifications. The "not new" limit appears three times near the top, and the middle instance adds nothing. The faithfulness limit is stated in full twice. One unexplained elevated term, "hard-oracle extreme", has a plain literal replacement available. Two smaller ordering issues are recorded as info: "the three precedents" is referenced before they are introduced, and consistency is relied on one paragraph before it is introduced. None of these issues affects placement or makes the article's conformance systematically fail, so the outcome is WARN.

# Review

The article is mostly economical for a lead piece that has to carry a worked example, a definition, a precedent sequence, a Bitter Lesson objection and an evidence section. Most of its restatements do a job. The three-point summary after the routing-line example turns the example into claims. The return to the "no built-in guarantee" point at the start of the success section turns it into the separate success test. The final failure condition turns the hazards into a falsifiable bet. None of these is flagged.

The redundancy is concentrated around the statement of the bet. The robust-comparison subsection says the same things in three paragraphs in a row: that the judge compares a pair and may leave it open, that reversibility lets the system act on an open comparison (with the routing line as the example), and that an action on an open comparison is a decision rather than a demonstrated improvement. The third paragraph adds only two sentences of new content. Those can be folded into the paragraph before it. Smaller repeats are a duplicated "not new" clause in the introduction and a recap sentence that closes the Gödel machine paragraph.

The hazard list's "unfaithful rationales" item repeats an earlier cost paragraph. It is marked INFO because the closing failure condition names that hazard, so the list entry may be needed as the anchor for that reference.

# Review

## Summary

The note has two core claims. The first is that selection needs only a
robust comparison, not one score. The second, and the article's distinctive
contribution, is the bet that a fixed-weight language model can derive the
preference model from a stated purpose and make that comparison. The first
claim is well developed: the decision-analysis account, the limit of the
analogy, and the treatment of open comparisons and reversibility.

The second claim is developed mostly as a statement of what the bet requires
and what it is not: reasons instead of explicit value functions, consistency,
and the double-loop requirement. Its first and novel step, building the
preference model from a purpose, gets no worked case. The worked example
mentions a weighing but skips the step where the admissible value functions
are identified. Meanwhile, the historical precedents (especially the Gödel
machine) and the Bitter Lesson rebuttal receive more detail than this step.

A fix need not cut the secondary material. Extending the routing-line example
would do it: name two or three value functions the purpose admits, and show
that they disagree on permanent adoption but agree on the trial. That would
give the load-bearing step concrete support. If the Bitter Lesson discussion
keeps growing, it could become its own article.

# Review

## Summary

I tested the note's frameworks against boundary cases. These were the two-part empirical check, the self-improvement ladder (learns by selection / self-improving / double-loop), the proof–formula–heuristics–robust-comparison progression, the comparison table, the hazard list and the judge's verdict space.

Most of them hold. The ladder handles its simplest case (an externally picked checkpoint) and its most extreme case (a team revising its own criteria). The table's contrast survives selection over weights, because the AlphaGo Zero example places checkpoint gating in the selection column. The precedent progression is used as an illustrative sequence, not a claimed taxonomy.

The clear gap is the operative-dependence test. The note defines a change to include removals, then states a test that presupposes a retained entry. Deletion, which is the note's own remedy for accretion, therefore falls outside the test as worded.

# Friction check: Deployment-Time Machine Learning: LLM-Selected Updates Without a Single Score

**Central claim (one sentence):** A deployed agent can learn by selecting edits to its readable instruction store through a robust comparison over a preference model instead of a single score, and the bet is that a fixed-weight LLM can autonomously build that preference model from a stated purpose, make the comparison, and revise its own criteria.

## Filter
**Filter:** SURVIVES

The properties the claim holds at once are: no single scalar, robust comparison (every compatible function agrees), an LLM that supplies reasons rather than computing over value functions, decisions on cases the comparison leaves open, and criterion revision under a fixed objective. These come close to colliding. With no stated preferences the note admits that robust comparison "leaves most real changes unordered". Open-ended objections can also widen the set, so much of the actual selection falls to decisions on open comparisons, not robust ones. The note avoids contradiction by keeping these decisions explicitly separate from improvement claims and making them reversible. It also does not claim that open-case decisions use no weighting, only that they are not reported as improvements. The claim therefore commits to one consistent thing. Its practical content, though, rests more on the open-case decision procedure than the title's "without a single score" suggests.

## Thinnest joints

The top joint is ranked first because it frames the whole bet: the article presents the judge as what turns an old process into a paradigm, but it never argues that the judge was the binding constraint, and its own limits section points elsewhere. The second and third joints are paired. The worked example is offered as establishing that no scalar was needed, but the robustness of the trial over leaving the file alone is the step that would make that true, and it is asserted, not traced. The Bitter Lesson placement is next: its categorical wording outruns the conditions the note attaches afterwards. The consistency test ranks lowest. Its logic is sound for strict robust preference and fails only through the conflation with open-case approval, which a short distinction would repair. The source-diagnosis passage about the harness-evolution study was considered but not surfaced. It is hedged enough ("though their single remedy run stayed within noise") that it does not bear the weight of a rebuttal.

## For the human
Look first at whether the routing-line trial is actually better than no change under every compatible measure. If it is not, the article's only worked case shows a decision on an open comparison, not the robust selection the title promises.

# Critique: Deployment-Time Machine Learning: LLM-Selected Updates Without a Single Score

**Note:** kb/articles/deployment-time-machine-learning-llm-selected-updates.md
**Central commitment:** A fixed-weight language model can do the selection step of double-loop selection-based learning over a readable store: it can derive a preference model from a declared purpose, make a robust comparison and decide the cases the comparison leaves open, so a deployed system can choose its updates without one scalar score.
**Critique mode:** claim
**Attack outcome:** partially lands

## Strongest case against it

An evaluation researcher working on LLM-as-judge, together with a decision theorist, would argue as follows. Once an LLM does the job, "robust comparison" is a relabeling with no operational content. It amounts to an LLM judge giving pairwise verdicts with reasons.

In the decision-analysis method the article borrows (Greco, Mousseau and Słowiński), two things produce robustness:

1. The set of compatible value functions is fixed by preferences stated outside the procedure.
2. Agreement across that set is computed, not asserted.

The article's bet drops both:

- **The model fixes the set.** The model "derive[s] the preference model from the declared purpose." The purpose is a short natural-language objective, and a stated purpose admits many sets of weightings. Nothing outside the model decides which set is the honest one. The linked necessary-preference note warns that narrowing the set to force agreement "smuggles a weighting back in." Under the bet, only the judge could detect that narrowing.
- **The model asserts agreement instead of computing it.** The article concedes that the model does not write down value functions and compute which option wins under all of them (lines 269–274). It offers "reasons that do the same work" instead. Reasons are not unanimity over a set. They are the stated grounds of a single verdict, and the article itself lists unfaithful rationales as a hazard.

So the distinctive claim, *robust* comparison and not just comparison, has no observable that would separate it from the null hypothesis: an LLM with one implicit, context-dependent weighting that sometimes hedges. The proposed consistency test does not separate them. A single-scalar judge also never approves a change and its reversal. The success test ("higher under every compatible measure") needs a set of compatible measures and does not say who supplies it:

- If people supply it, the bet's novel part, the model building the preference model, goes untested.
- If the model supplies it, the test is circular.

The worked example does not exercise the claim either. The judge resolves the routing line by trial adoption, a reversibility-based decision. Its lesson that "no single scalar metric had to be invented" holds for any LLM judge. The opponent concludes that the title's "without a single score" describes the absence of an *explicit* score, not the presence of a robust comparison. The paradigm then reduces to "use an LLM as judge in an edit loop," which is neither new nor addressed by the decision-theory framing.

## How the note engages it

**Partially engaged.** The note anticipates part of the attack:

- **Model does not compute value functions.** It disclaims that the model computes over value functions and offers checkable reasons instead (lines 269–274).
- **Capability, not mechanism.** It says the procedure "says what the judge must do, not how its weights produce an answer." It concedes that "even consistent answers can neglect a cost the stated purpose requires the judge to count" (lines 276–280).
- **Open verdicts stay open.** It reports open verdicts as decisions, not improvements (lines 283–284 and 352–356).
- **Consistency test.** It proposes testing for cycles (lines 286–288).
- **Hazards.** It lists judgment reliability and unfaithful rationales as hazards (lines 383–391).
- **Empirical framing.** It frames the whole claim as a bet with no completed run (lines 375–378). This blunts any charge that it claims success.

The note does not engage the core of the attack, the independence problem: what fixes the compatible set other than the judge. It also gives no observable that tells a robust-comparison judge from a single-weighting judge. Its claim that the reasons "can be checked and challenged one at a time" is stronger than its own cited source. That source says the weighing part of such reasons cannot be checked independently. The worked example's third lesson credits the absence of a scalar to a decision that was actually settled by reversibility.

The attack does not fully land, because the article states a bet rather than a result and says explicitly that the judge need not compute. The bet as worded is still falsifiable in principle. But because no test separates its distinctive part from plain LLM judgment, the decision-theory framing currently adds vocabulary rather than a testable difference.

## Constructive findings

- **Say what fixes compatibility.** State what, independent of the judging model, constrains which measures are compatible. Candidates: stated preferences elicited from people beforehand, retained precedents, or a separate critic whose objections can widen the set. Then say which parts of the preference model the bet claims the model can supply without that constraint.
- **Separate the bet from the null.** Name an observable that tells the bet apart from a single-weighting LLM judge. For example: the judge returns "open" on exactly those pairs where independently fixed admissible weightings disagree, and the weightings it names as reversing its choice really do reverse it when checked.
- **Keep the source's limit.** Change "Those reasons can be checked and challenged one at a time" to keep the necessary-preference note's limit: factual parts can be checked, but the weighing cannot be checked independently of who offered it.
- **Say who supplies the measures in tests.** In the success test, or by an explicit pointer to the testing article, say who supplies the compatible measures in an evaluation run, and whether that leaves the model's preference-building untested.
- **Fix the worked example.** Either reword the third lesson so it credits the trial decision to reversibility, or add one case in which the robust comparison itself decides. An example would be a change that wins under every plausible loss-to-gain ratio.

## Secondary objections (optional)

- **Bitter Lesson placement.** The Bitter Lesson section places the system "on the computation side" once an LLM supplies the comparison. But the declared purpose, and therefore the first constraints on the preference model, stay human-supplied. The bootstrap condition at lines 335–338 covers hand-written instructions and gates, but not the purpose that seeds every comparison. The article could say whether supplying the purpose counts as human domain knowledge under the lesson.
- **Mixed evidence label.** Calling the paradigm "Deployment-Time Machine Learning" while also saying that software teams maintaining handbooks do the same process invites the reply that the only new element is the LLM judge. That is the element the main attack says the article has not yet made testable.

# Premise decomposition: Deployment-Time Machine Learning: LLM-Selected Updates Without a Single Score

**Register:** claim
**Central commitment (one sentence):** A deployed system can learn at deployment time by selecting edits to a readable store through a robust comparison across a preference model rather than a single score, and (the empirical bet) a fixed-weight LLM can build that preference model from a declared purpose and make the comparison, including diagnosing and revising its own criteria.

## Premises and counterexamples

The commitment has two layers, and the premises split along them.

The first layer is the paradigm claim. Selection needs only a local comparison, and robust comparison supplies it without a chosen weighting. Its premises are the sufficiency of local comparison, robust comparison doing the selecting, the worked example's demonstration, the contrast with direct gradient training, and the historical precedents.
